title: Tension, compression, and stiffness
summary: See how a truss carries a load, and why a stiffer material changes the deflection but not the forces.

steps.title: Tension and compression
steps.text:
A truss carries loads through members that are pulled (tension, red) or pushed (compression, blue). Solve the simple triangle, which has a 20 kN load at the top.

The two sloping members are in compression and the base is in tension. Why does each sloping member carry more than half of the load?

check.hint: Load the setup, then press Solve.
check.success: Each sloping member leans at 60°, so only part of its force holds the load up: 20 kN / (2 sin 60°) = 11.5 kN. The base ties their outward push together.

steps.title: A bridge truss
steps.text: The Pratt truss is a classic bridge design: diagonals in tension and verticals in compression. Solve it and look at the Model and Member forces tabs.

check.success: About 36 kN in the most loaded members.

steps.title: Stiffer material
steps.text:
Doubling Young's modulus E makes the truss twice as stiff. Open the Sections tab: every member uses section S1. Type 400 into its E (GPa) (the material becomes Custom), and solve again.

The largest displacement halves to about 0.116 mm, but the member forces do not change: this truss is statically determinate, so equilibrium alone sets the forces.

check.hint: Sections tab: set S1's E to 400, then Solve.
check.success: Half the deflection, the same forces.

steps.title: Forces in proportion
steps.text: The truss is linear: double every load and every force doubles. Sweep the Load scale from 0.5 to 4 (the Analyze ▸ Sweep tab is set up) and plot Largest tension: a straight line through the origin.
